# Results — Study 350 (Dartboard-Portfolio) on a real mega-cap tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The Malkiel dartboard run as
a cross-sectional race: from a 20-name US mega-cap universe, **500 blindfolded monkeys**
each pick **k = 10** names at random and hold them equal-weight (re-drawing every year),
raced against the **cap-weighted index** of the same universe, an **equal-weight index**
(the size-tilt control), and a concentrated **expert** (the 10 largest names). Monthly
total-return data, annual rebalance. As-of **2026-05-31** (the last full month — the
in-progress June bar is dropped); match the fingerprint to confirm you hold the same tape.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Universe | 20 current US mega-caps (AAPL, MSFT, AMZN, … DIS) |
| Window | 2013-02-28 → 2026-05-31 (160 months) |
| Fingerprint | `212217b18220` |
| Source | Yahoo! Finance total-return monthly; cap snapshot via `fast_info` |

> **Survivorship & point-in-time caveats (named on the Signal axis).** The universe is
> *current* membership projected back, and the cap weights are a *current* snapshot, not
> point-in-time. Both biases flatter the largest survivors — i.e. they help the
> cap-weighted index, the leg the dartboard loses to here. The qualitative finding (the
> dartboard ≈ the equal-weight index, not skill) is robust to this; the exact margin is
> not. This is an upper bound on the cap index, hence a *lower* bound on the dartboard.

## The headline — the race (gross, annual rebalance)

| Strategy | CAGR | Sharpe | max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **Cap-weighted index** | **+33.50%** | 1.56 | −33.7% |
| Expert (10 largest, EW) | +28.38% | 1.55 | −27.1% |
| Equal-weight index | +20.59% | 1.43 | −18.6% |
| **Median dartboard (500 monkeys)** | **+20.27%** | 1.41 | −19.1% |

- **The monkey loses.** On this mega-cap universe over 2013–2026, the median dartboard
  trails the cap-weighted index by **−11.67%/yr**, HAC *t* = **−3.66** (n = 160 months),
  block-bootstrap 95% CI on the monthly spread **[−147, −47] bps** — entirely below zero.
- **Win-rate vs the cap index: 0.0%** (0 of 500 monkeys beat it). Vs the expert: **0.0%**.
- **The dartboard is just the equal-weight index with extra noise.** Median dart minus the
  *equal-weight* index is **−0.26%/yr** (*t* = −2.17) — a sliver of drag from the random
  10-name subsampling and turnover, nothing more. The dartboard's entire performance is
  its (here-losing) **size tilt**, not stock-picking.

## Why the famous result reverses here — it was always a size tilt

The Wall Street Journal contest and the Research Affiliates "monkey" study found random
portfolios *beating* the cap-weighted index. That is real — but mechanical: random
equal-weight selection over-weights the many smaller names the cap index barely holds, so
whenever **small beats large** (the size premium), the monkey wins. Our universe is the
opposite case: **mega-caps led the 2013–2026 decade**, so cap-weighting concentrated into
exactly the winners (AAPL/MSFT/NVDA), and the size tilt the monkey carries became a
*headwind*. The dartboard's relative result flips sign with the universe and the regime —
which is the proof it was never skill.

## Cost sweep — turnover is not the binding constraint here

The dartboard's full annual re-draw is high turnover (~100% one-way per rebalance), but
on this tape the monkey already loses gross, so costs only widen the gap:

| round-trip cost | dartboard win-rate vs cap index | median dart − cap, HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | 0.0% | −3.66 |
| 10 bps/leg | 0.0% | −3.69 |
| 25 bps/leg | 0.0% | −3.74 |
| 50 bps/leg | 0.0% | −3.81 |

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is a faithful size-tilt detector

On a deterministic synthetic panel with a *planted* small-cap premium, the dartboard's
edge over the cap index rises monotonically with the premium — while its difference from
the **equal-weight index stays at ~0 throughout**, confirming the edge is the size tilt,
never selection skill:

| planted size premium | dart win-rate vs cap index | dart − cap (HAC *t*) | dart − equal index (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.000 (null) | 30.0% | −0.89 | −0.46 |
| 0.002 | 65.0% | +1.33 | −0.30 |
| 0.004 | 89.5% | +3.58 | −0.20 |
| 0.006 (strong) | 99.5% | +5.84 | −0.15 |

At the null the monkey neither wins nor loses against the cap index in expectation
(*t* = −0.89, insignificant); plant a size premium and it "beats" the index — but it never
beats the equal-weight index, because that already holds the tilt the monkey is renting.

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** The dartboard-vs-cap-index spread is statistically real on our tape
  (HAC *t* = −3.66), but it is *negative* here and, decisively, the dartboard is
  statistically indistinguishable from the equal-weight index (−0.26%/yr). "Random picking
  beats the index" is not a stable real effect — it is a universe-dependent **size tilt**
  that here points the other way. The literature supports the size mechanism; the *skill*
  claim has no real-tape support.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no stock-picking edge to harvest — only a known
  size/concentration tilt (here a loser) carried at high random-rebalance turnover.
- **A blindfolded monkey beats the pros (skill)? — BUSTED.** The monkey tracks the
  equal-weight index, not the experts' alpha. On a mega-cap universe in a mega-cap decade
  it loses to both the index and the expert, 0 of 500 throws.
